title: DNA replication; Gene mutations
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Edexcel A-level Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: GE01b#t4 term and clue written for the game; GE06a#t3 term and clue written for the game; GE06a#t2 term and clue written for the game; GE06a#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: GE01b#N.7, GE06a#N.3, GE01b#N.9, GE06a#N.6a, GE01b#N.10, GE06a#N.11.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Hybrid DNA
items.clue: Intermediate band: one ¹⁵N strand paired with one ¹⁴N strand.

items.label: Deletion
items.clue: Loss of a base from the sequence, leaving it one base shorter.

items.label: Substitution
items.clue: One base is replaced by another, so the sequence stays the same length.

items.label: Gene mutation
items.clue: A change in the base sequence of DNA, often an uncorrected copying error.

questions.stem: A double-stranded DNA molecule in which both strands contain only heavy nitrogen (¹⁵N) is replicated three times in a medium that supplies only light nitrogen (¹⁴N), producing 8 DNA molecules. How many of the 8 DNA molecules contain any ¹⁵N?

options.text: 1 of 8
8 of 8
2 of 8
4 of 8

questions.explanation: In round 1 the two ¹⁵N strands separate and each pairs with a new ¹⁴N strand. They stay intact in every later round, so after round 3, 2 molecules contain ¹⁵N and 6 contain only ¹⁴N.

questions.stem: Part of the base sequence of a gene is GAT TCA GGC ATT before a mutation and GAT TCG GCA TT after it. Which type of gene mutation has occurred?

options.text: A substitution of the base A by G at the sixth position in the sequence
A chromosome mutation, because the total amount of DNA has changed
A deletion of one base, which has moved every later base one position along
A substitution that has shifted the reading frame of later codons

questions.explanation: The A in the second codon is missing and every base after it has moved up one place; the mutant is one base shorter. This is a deletion.

questions.stem: In the Meselson–Stahl experiment, which result after one generation in ¹⁴N would have supported the conservative model?

options.text: One band, of intermediate density.
Two bands of equal amount, one heavy and one light.
One band, heavy.
Two bands of equal amount, one intermediate and one light.

questions.explanation: Conservative keeps the parent molecule whole (heavy) and makes a completely new one (light): two bands, equal amounts.

questions.stem: In mRNA the codons GCU, GCC, GCA and GCG all code for alanine. A base substitution in a gene changes the codon GCU in its mRNA to GCC. What is the effect on the polypeptide?

options.text: Alanine is replaced by a different amino acid at that one position
None: the same amino acid, alanine, is placed at that position
The reading frame shifts, changing all amino acids after it
Every amino acid in the polypeptide is changed to another one

questions.explanation: GCC codes for alanine just as GCU does. Because the code is degenerate, a base substitution may or may not change a single amino acid.

questions.stem: The experiment is run in reverse. Bacteria are grown for many generations on light nitrogen (¹⁴N), then moved to a medium containing only heavy nitrogen (¹⁵N). Replication is semi-conservative. What will the DNA show after two generations on ¹⁵N?

options.text: Two bands of equal amount: intermediate and light.
Two bands of equal amount: intermediate and heavy.
One band, between intermediate and heavy.
Two bands: one quarter light, three quarters heavy.

questions.explanation: Generation 1: every molecule is one light + one heavy strand (intermediate). Generation 2: 4 molecules, 2 hybrids holding the old light strands and 2 all-heavy.

questions.stem: In the allele that causes sickle cell anaemia, the mRNA codon for amino acid 6 of the beta chain of haemoglobin is GUG instead of GAG. GAG codes for glutamic acid and GUG codes for valine. What is the effect of this mutation on the protein?

options.text: One amino acid out of more than a hundred is changed, too small a difference to alter the structure or function of haemoglobin.
The reading frame is shifted from this codon onward, so every amino acid after it in the beta chain is different.
The codon GUG is degenerate, so the ribosome can still insert glutamic acid and the haemoglobin produced is normal.
Valine replaces glutamic acid at one position, which alters haemoglobin enough for it to form fibres at low oxygen concentrations.
